Entryway.alt: The same entryway drawn twice, side by side. On the left, labelled before, coats crowd a single rail, a scarf trails to the floor, shoes lie loose across a curling mat, and a console disappears under mail, cables, a power strip and a phone on charge. On the right, labelled after, four coats hang evenly with hooks left free, a basket and plant sit on the shelf above, the console holds only a tray with keys and glasses and one upright file of paper, shoes are paired on a low rack under a bench, and a flat mat sits square inside the door on clear floor.

A warm overhead plan of an entryway with its five zones outlined and numbered. Zone one, the landing spot, is a console by the wall holding keys, a phone and sunglasses. Zone two, the coats, is a shelf and hook rail with four coats and a bag. Zone three, the shoes, is a rack of paired shoes with a boot tray beside it. Zone four, the bench or console, is a cushioned bench. Zone five, the door, mat, and immediate floor, is the door with its swing arc drawn as a dashed line across the mat and the strip of floor inside it. A line beneath reads: one room, five small jobs.

A coat rail photographed against a pale wall, titled Coat Storage Standard, one hook per person, two empty hooks for guests. Six coats hang evenly spaced with two hooks deliberately left empty at the end. Callouts read: one hook per person, today's jacket lives here; seasonal items, store off-season coats elsewhere, keep only what you use now; two empty hooks, always keep two hooks open for guests. A side panel headed The Standard lists: space hooks evenly so coats do not touch; keep coats off the floor; use the hook that matches the person who owns it; guests always have a place; a calm rack makes a calm home. Baskets beneath the bench are labelled hats and gloves, scarves, and rain gear.

A shoe rack and boot tray photographed beside a front door, titled Shoe Zone Standard, daily shoes have a home, wet shoes stay on the tray. Four pairs sit paired and facing the same way on an open shelf, with boots and wet footwear below on a raised black tray. Callouts read: daily shoes only, only the shoes you wear this week live here; shoes paired, pairs stay together and face the same direction; boot tray, all wet, snowy or muddy shoes stay on the tray, the floor stays dry and clean; clear path, keep the walking path open, nothing on the floor outside the tray zone. A dashed arrow across the floor is labelled traffic flow. A side panel headed The Standard lists: daily shoes on the shelf; boots on the tray; no shoes in the walkway; tray and floor easy to clean; everyone can find their shoes in seconds.

A hall bench and console photographed beneath a round mirror, titled Bench / Console Standard, surfaces clear, storage hidden, style simple. The top holds only a lamp, a small tray, a plant and one framed picture. Three lidless baskets sit on the shelf below, labelled hats and gloves, scarves, and rain gear. Callouts read: clear surface, keep the top completely clear for daily use; hidden storage, baskets or bins hide the clutter and keep things categorized; decorate with restraint, use one tray, a plant, and one personal item; label everything, labels make it easy for everyone to put things back in the right place; bench ready, if the bench has a cushion or seat, keep it clear and usable. A panel headed The Standard reads: top surface is clear and easy to use; everything else has a home and is hidden from view; the bench is ready for a seat or a bag.

Kitchen.alt: The same kitchen photographed in two states side by side. On the left, labelled before, the counter is crowded with a coffee maker, a kettle, jars, mugs, a water bottle and a drift of mail and papers, cloths are draped over the counter edge, and the sink is full. On the right, labelled after, the same kitchen is clear and clean: the counter holds only a board, a small plant and a bottle of oil, the shelves above are ordered with stacked bowls and plates, the sink is empty and dry, the hob and hood are clean, and a bowl of apples sits on the far counter.

A prep counter photographed before and after cleaning, titled Primary Prep Counter Before / After. On the before side, numbered callouts read: appliances trap crumbs under and behind; backsplash seam collects grease and grit; crumbs and spills become sticky when ignored; counter edge collects drips and debris. On the after side the counter is bare and bright, with notes reading clean seam no buildup, clear workspace for safe efficient food prep, and edge is clean and dry. A panel headed what changes everything lists: remove appliances and clean underneath, clean the backsplash seam thoroughly, wipe scrub and degrease the entire surface, and clean the front edge and underside lip.

A close view of a counter edge and backsplash, titled Counter Edge Inspection, the small places hold the big problems. Five numbered callouts mark the underside lip where dust and crumbs collect under the front edge, the backsplash seam where grease creeps into the smallest gaps, scorch marks where heat and spills leave stains, caulk condition where cracked or missing caulk lets moisture in, and edge buildup where hard-to-see grime hides along the edges. A side panel adds that running your hand along edges and seams tells you whether they need attention.

A gas hob with the grates removed, titled Cleaning the Burner Wells, the hidden zone where grease builds and performance suffers. Numbered callouts mark the grease ring collecting around the burner base, the igniter to wipe gently without bending, the gas ports to clear with a detail brush, the knob stems where grease and spills collect, and the burner well itself. A six-step strip shows removing grates and caps, brushing away loose crumbs, spraying degreaser onto a cloth rather than directly onto igniters or ports, wiping and scrubbing all surfaces, using swabs around the igniters and gas ports, and wiping dry.

A tiled backsplash behind a hob shown half dirty and half clean, titled Backsplash and Grout Lines. Callouts on the dirty half mark cooking splatter dried onto the tiles, a sticky grease film that collects dust and looks dull, and grout grime where grease and food particles settle into the lines. A six-step strip shows spraying degreaser onto a microfiber cloth and not directly onto the tile, wiping the tiles, scrubbing the grout lines with a detail brush, treating tough grout with a baking soda paste, wiping clean with a damp cloth, and finishing with a dry cloth.

A double stainless sink and mixer tap, titled Sink and Faucet. Numbered callouts mark the faucet where water spots and soap scum build around the base, handle and spout, the backsplash line where drips leave residue where the counter meets the wall, the basin surfaces where food scraps and hard water spots stick, the drain and strainer where trapped food causes odours and slow drains, and the rim and edges where water and grime collect underneath. A six-step strip runs from spraying cleaner and letting it sit through scrubbing the drain with a brush to drying with a microfiber cloth for a streak-free finish.

Kitchen cabinets shown closed and open side by side, titled Cabinets Inside and Out. On the outside, callouts mark fingerprints on high-touch areas, dust and grease on the top edges of doors and drawers, and grease around the base and crevices of handles and knobs. On the inside, callouts mark dust settling on top interior surfaces, spills and crumbs along the front shelf edges, and crumbs and dust building up in hinges and tight corners. A six-step strip shows spraying degreaser onto a cloth rather than the cabinets, wiping top edges then fronts working top to bottom, cleaning handles and knobs, removing items and wiping inside, using a detail brush in the hinges, and wiping shelf surfaces and front edges before letting them dry and restocking.

Pantry.alt: A three-step photographic sequence titled Dry Before Wet, subtitled vacuum or brush first, wipe second, dry last. Step one, dry, remove loose debris: a vacuum crevice brush lifting spilled flour from a pantry shelf beside glass jars of oats, rice and pasta. Step two, wet, wipe clean: a hand wiping the same shelf with a damp green microfiber cloth. Step three, dry, dry completely: a hand drying the shelf with a white cloth. A panel headed inspect after drying says to look in corners, along seams and behind containers, and that the surface should be clean, dry and squeaky. A warning panel headed flour plus water equals paste explains that wiping flour with a wet cloth turns it into sticky paste that hides dirt, attracts pests, and is harder to clean.

An overhead photograph of the pantry cleaning kit laid out on an oak surface, titled Pantry Cleaning Kit, gather everything before you start. Each item is labelled: a vacuum with a crevice attachment and a brush attachment, a detail brush, a bottle brush, a plain bottle of mild dish soap, a plain amber bottle of multi-surface cleaner, a stack of colour-coded microfiber cloths, a roll of labels, a permanent marker, three airtight containers holding flour, sugar and pasta, a wooden shelf riser, and a clear turntable. All containers and bottles are plain and unbranded.

A six-step photographic sequence titled Dry Goods Shelf Cleaning Sequence, subtitled clean in this order, dry first, wet second, dry last. Step one, remove everything: the shelf contents grouped on a counter. Step two, vacuum loose debris: a vacuum crevice brush lifting flour and crumbs from the empty shelf. Step three, brush corners and edges: a wooden detail brush working a shelf corner. Step four, wipe with a damp cloth, with a note to spray onto the cloth and not the shelf. Step five, dry completely with a clean dry cloth so nothing is left damp. Step six, inspect and reload, showing labelled airtight containers returned to a clean shelf. An inspection checklist runs along the foot: corners clean and dry, seams and shelf pins clean, no sticky residue, no flour paste, no pests or signs of activity, no water marks or damp spots.

Dining Room.alt: The same dining room photographed in two states side by side. On the left, labelled before, the table is lost under a laptop, stacked papers, mugs, plates and bags, a coat is draped over a chair back, a handbag hangs from another, and the sideboard behind is crowded with post and clutter. On the right, labelled after, the identical room from the identical angle is calm: the table is bare wood holding only a tray with a small plant and a candle, every chair is pushed in, the sideboard is clear, and the china cabinet beyond is ordered.

A warm overhead plan of a dining room with its five zones outlined, numbered and named. Zone one, the dining table, is the table at the centre of the room with its chairs. Zone two, the sideboard surface, is the top of the long sideboard against the far wall. Zone three, the sideboard storage, is the drawers and cabinets of a second unit along the left wall. Zone four, the china cabinet, is the tall glass-fronted cabinet on the right. Zone five, the beverage station, is a small unit with a coffee machine in the lower right corner. Solid and dashed arrows mark the primary walking paths and secondary movement around the table. A line reads: one room, five manageable jobs.

A reference table titled Match the Touch to the Finish, with a column for each surface. Oak wood, described as natural sealed wood, takes a soft microfiber cloth and a pH neutral wood cleaner, and avoids ammonia, bleach and all-purpose cleaners. Glass takes a lint-free glass cloth and glass cleaner, and avoids paper towels which leave lint and scratches. Silver, which tarnishes and scratches easily, takes a soft polishing cloth and silver polish as needed, and avoids abrasive pads and steel wool. Fine china, at chip and crack risk, takes a soft dish towel and mild dish soap in warm water, and avoids the dishwasher because it causes chips and cracks. Veneer, a thin wood layer, takes a soft microfiber cloth and pH neutral wood cleaner, and avoids ammonia, bleach and oily furniture sprays.

An overhead photograph of the dining room care kit laid out on a pale surface, with eleven numbered items: a plain bottle labelled neutral cleaner for wood, veneer and sealed surfaces; a plain bottle labelled glass cleaner; a stack of colour-coded microfiber cloths; a soft detailing brush for corners, carvings and seams; a plastic scraper for sticky residue; a plain tin labelled silver polish; a dish basin for hand-washing china and crystal; soft towels; vacuum upholstery and crevice attachments; cotton swabs and pipe cleaners for tight spaces; and cotton gloves for handling fine china and silver. A panel below shows everything gathered in a small wooden caddy.

A photograph of a set dining room titled Dining Table Reset, subtitled a table with one job: bring people together. Callouts on the left list what the ideal table excludes: no mail or papers, because paperwork invites clutter back; no devices, because the table is for connection not screens; no bags or backpacks, which should be given a home elsewhere; a clear surface; and chairs in place, all pushed in to show the table is finished. Callouts on the right mark a simple centerpiece of one natural element, and a note that a clear table means you can seat guests in ten minutes.

A photograph of a long oak sideboard titled Sideboard Organization Strategy, subtitled separate serving space from display. The left two thirds of the top is outlined and labelled the serving run, kept clear for serving, buffets and everyday needs. The right third is outlined and labelled the display area, holding a framed picture, a bowl, a small stack of books, a plant and a lamp grouped together. A side panel notes that everything on the sideboard should serve, display, or support, and that anything else should be relocated.

A photograph of an open sideboard titled Ideal Sideboard Storage, subtitled everything has a visible home, easy to find, easy to return. Detail circles show the top left drawer holding linens and napkins rolled or folded so everything is visible; the top right drawer holding serving utensils organised by type with handles facing the same direction; the left cabinet holding platters and trays stored vertically; the centre cabinet holding serveware and bowls grouped by type; the right top holding silver and flatware in felt-lined trays or cloth wraps to prevent tarnish; and the right bottom holding tablecloths, candles and chargers used less often.

Living Room.alt: The same living room photographed in two states side by side. On the left, labelled before, clothes and blankets are strewn across both sofas, the coffee table is buried under magazines, mugs, papers and a games controller, cups and remotes cover the side table, and items are scattered across the floor and rug. On the right, labelled after, the identical room from the identical angle is calm: both sofas are clear with cushions squared, the coffee table holds only a tray with a small plant, the side table holds one book and a plant, the shelves are ordered, and the floor and rug are completely clear.

A photograph of a living room titled Hidden Dirt Map, with fourteen labelled callouts marking the places dust collects out of sight: curtain rods, tops of bookshelves, tops of books, behind the sofa along the wall and ledge, behind the television where dust and hair affect airflow and heat, the lamp bulb and shade where dust reduces brightness, under the sofa cushions where crumbs, hair and dust hide, the sofa seams and arms where dust, oils and skin cells collect, the electronic vents where dust blocks airflow and causes heat, the baseboards and corners, under the coffee table, under the rug, and under the furniture.

A reference table titled Match the Tool to the Surface, with a row for each surface. Screens, meaning televisions, monitors and tablets, take a dry microfiber cloth only, wiped gently in straight lines, because screens scratch easily and are damaged by liquids; do not spray anything on the screen and use no paper towels. Vents on the television, media console and registers take a brush attachment and vacuum, brushing first to loosen and vacuuming to remove, because dust blocks airflow and causes electronics to overheat. Wood takes a barely damp microfiber cloth wiped with the grain. Glass takes glass cleaner sprayed on the cloth and not on the glass. Fabric takes the upholstery attachment, worked slowly with overlapping passes. Lamps take a soft brush and a dry cloth with the bulb cool and off.

Family Room.alt: A media console photographed before and after cleaning, titled Media Center Before and After, subtitled clear vents, organized cables, controllers docked, everything has a home. On the before side, numbered callouts mark dust blocking the console vents, cables tangled and hard to clean, and controllers lying loose with no home, with a note that dust causes heat and tangled cables collect more dust. On the after side the identical console is clean: the vents are clear so air can flow, the cables are contained and labelled in a covered channel, and the controllers stand in a dock, with a note that clear vents help electronics last longer. A tip at the foot says to dust the console and shelves weekly and keep airflow clear on all sides and the back.

Primary Bedroom.alt: The same primary bedroom photographed in two states side by side. On the left, labelled before, clothes cover the unmade bed and the bench at its foot, a dresser drawer hangs open with garments spilling out, shoes and a charging cable lie across the floor between the door and the bed, and the dresser top is crowded with bottles and clutter. On the right, labelled after, the identical room from the identical angle is calm: the bed is made with smooth linen, the dresser top holds only a small tray and a vase, both nightstands are clear, and the strip of floor from the door to the bed is completely bare.

A photograph of a finished primary bedroom titled What Makes a Finished Bedroom, with ten numbered callouts. A made bed that is smooth, simple and inviting. Clear walls with nothing extra. Five-item nightstands holding a lamp, water, something to read, glasses and one personal item and no more. A dresser top with one tray and one purpose. Hidden cords so charging happens out of sight. A clear path so you can walk from door to bed in the dark without tripping. A clear space under the bed. A seating zone for putting on shoes or setting out tomorrow's clothes. Organized drawers with one category per drawer. And natural light from open shades in the morning.

A seven step vertical sequence titled Clean for Sleep, Not Appearance, subtitled a sleep-first cleaning sequence for a healthier bedroom, with a side note reading you do not just clean the bedroom, you clean what touches you while you sleep. Step one, wash your sheets weekly to remove sweat, oils, skin cells and dust. Step two, wash pillow protectors, which block sweat, oils and allergens from reaching your pillows. Step three, wash pillows seasonally, following the care label. Step four, air your mattress by stripping the bed, opening windows and letting it breathe. Step five, air your duvet, because fresh air removes moisture and odours you cannot see. Step six, remake your bed. Step seven, finish with a reset: clear the surfaces, open the curtains, invite light.

A photograph of a bedroom titled Hidden Dirt in the Bedroom, subtitled the places dust, skin cells and allergens love to hide, with a warning line reading out of sight does not mean clean. Nine callouts with magnified detail circles mark: behind the headboard where dust settles night after night; under the bed where dust, hair and lint build up fast out of sight; mattress seams and tufts where skin cells, sweat and dust mites collect; dresser gaps and corners including top edges and drawer tracks; between furniture and walls, in the gaps around nightstands and dressers; the closet rod where dust, lint and skin cells build up; the closet back wall where dust collects on the wall and in the corners; and floor edges and corners along the baseboards and under the door swing.

A photograph of a stripped bed titled Mattress Airing Method, subtitled fresh air removes moisture, odours and dust so you sleep cleaner. The mattress stands upright on its side against the wall beside an open window, the duvet is draped over a wooden rack, and two pillows stand upright on the bare slats. Three callouts explain: air the mattress by standing it up or removing all bedding, opening windows and letting it breathe; air the duvet by draping it over a rack or clean surface so both sides get airflow; and air the pillows by standing them upright so moisture escapes and the filling stays fluffy. A side panel notes that fresh air, natural light and airflow do the heavy lifting with no products needed, and that a cross-breeze is best.

Guest Bedroom.alt: The same guest bedroom photographed in two states side by side. On the left, labelled before and captioned a forgotten room full of overflow, the bed is buried under stacks of folded clothes and a storage tub, cardboard boxes and bags are piled on the floor, a laundry basket sits beside an exercise bike, and the dresser top is crowded. On the right, labelled after and captioned guest ready, fresh, welcoming, the identical room from the identical angle holds a made bed with a folded throw, a luggage rack at its foot, a clear desk with a lamp and a small plant, a clear dresser top, and a completely clear path from the door to the bed.

A photograph of a guest bedroom titled Fresh Air Matters, subtitled fresh air removes stale odours, resets the room, and wakes up fabrics. Four numbered callouts: open the window to invite in fresh air and natural light; air the room by letting the curtains move and the room breathe; open storage by opening drawers and closet doors for better air flow; and airing linens by taking them out of storage and letting them breathe. In the photograph the casement window stands open with the curtains lifting, three dresser drawers are pulled open, the closet door is open, and a stack of folded linens sits airing on the bed. A note reads that air is the cheapest, easiest and most effective reset for any guest room.

A five step photographic sequence titled Air the Linens, subtitled stored linens can trap moisture and odours, airing them brings back freshness. Step one, remove and unfold, taking linens out of storage and unfolding completely. Step two, shake it out, giving each piece a good shake to loosen and refresh. Step three, air it well, hanging or draping linens in a well ventilated space. Step four, check for freshness, letting linens air for at least thirty minutes and longer if needed. Step five, fold and store, folding neatly and returning to storage inside a pillowcase set. A footer lists the best places to air linens: near an open window, on a drying rack, outside in the shade, and in the bathroom with the fan on.

A six panel photographic checklist titled Test Everything Before Guests Arrive, subtitled a few minutes of testing prevents frustration in the dark. One, turn on the lamp and check that it works and the bulb is the right brightness. Two, test all charging cables by plugging in each one to make sure it charges a phone. Three, check the power outlets are working and not blocked by furniture. Four, confirm wifi access by connecting to the network and verifying the password. Five, check the alarm clock by setting the time and confirming the alarm works. Six, replace batteries if needed in the remote and clock.

A six step photographic sequence titled Mattress Refresh Procedure. Step one, vacuum thoroughly using an upholstery attachment over the entire top surface including seams and tufts. Step two, check and spot clean, inspecting for stains and blotting rather than rubbing. Step three, rotate the mattress one hundred and eighty degrees head to foot to reduce body impressions. Step four, protect the mattress with a clean protector against spills, sweat and dust mites. Step five, check the foundation for dust, debris or anything loose and tighten screws if needed. Step six, make it inviting with fresh linens and a smooth top sheet.

A before and after pair titled Empty Drawers Welcome Guests. The before, labelled cluttered drawer, shows a nightstand drawer full of cables, sunglasses, tins, a notebook, a torch and assorted household oddments, with a note that when drawers are full guests have nowhere to put their items and it signals the room is still in use. The after, labelled empty drawer, shows the same drawer completely empty. A footer lists what guests typically use drawer space for: clothes, small items, toiletries, books and personal items.

A photograph of a woven welcome tray on a made bed titled Small Details, Big Welcome. The tray holds a small plant, a welcome card, a bottle of water, a notebook and pen, and two plain unbranded snacks. Six numbered extras are listed alongside: water, a snack, a fresh touch such as a plant, soft light from a working lamp, an extra towel or blanket, and a short welcome note. A footer shows five places to put welcome touches: a basket on the bed, the nightstand, the closet shelf, the bathroom counter, and the dresser or table.
